## Overview {#sec-overview}

Litter and neighborhood cleanliness are important social determinants of health that can negatively impact the safety and health of a city’s residents (1). In Philadelphia litter was ranked as the second most pressing issue in the city by residents (2). This project aims to understand how litter is distributed throughout the city and which areas may be disproportionately impacted by a high litter presence.

Ashley Butago, a Jr. Data Analyst at the Institute of Biomedical Informatics was consulted for this project and helped identify a potential need for reverse geocoding of the dataset and relevant tools for this task. Amy Yang, a Research Specialist, was also consulted for this project and helped guide the project design and analysis.

<https://github.com/clairegl/BMIN5030_Final_Project>

## Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Social determinants of health are made up of the condition a person lives in that impacts their health. They are non-medical and largely consist of social, environmental, and personal factors such as a person’s built environment, economic situation, and level of education. Included in this is litter, a component of a person's physical environment. It is important for a city to have proper sanitation as it is a key part of the health and safety of residents (1) and while the presence of litter can affect all residents of a place it has been shown to disproportionately impact lower income, vulnerable communities (6). Some types of litter such as broken glass can injure residents (3) while other types of litter such as food scraps can feed pests like cockroaches and rats (1). Additionally, litter not only has a physical impact but a psychological one as well. Pervasive litter influences resident’s perceptions of how safe and welcoming the area they live in is, decreasing satisfaction with their living conditions (5).

In Philadelphia specifically, it was rated as the second most pressing issue of the city by residents (2). Highlighting the attitudes of and urgency around addressing the city’s litter problem and improving sanitation. Thus, the goal of this project is to map the distribution of Philadelphia's litter by census tract and how litter presence correlates to the median household income, education and other indicators of wealth and vulnrability in order to understand which parts of the city may be disproportionately impacted by litter and where city sanitation efforts should be directed.

This project aims to answer the following research questions:

RQ1: How is litter distributed throughout Philadelphia?

RQ2: How is the distribution of litter correlated to median household income, median home value, and other indicators of wealth and vulnerability?

The issue of litter’s impact on health is more than a public health issue. It is an interdisciplinary issue that can draw from environmental, urban planning, and data science perspectives. Addressing this issue requires collaboration with those from different disciplines. Consulted in this project were two staff members Ashley Butago and Amy Yang. Butago is a Jr. Data Analyst at the Institute of Biomedical Informatics. She helped with understanding the dataset, identified a potential need for reverse geocoding of the dataset, and suggested relevant APIs and R packages for this task. Yang is a Research Specialist in the Guo Lab. She helped with guiding the project design, suggested different types of analysis for this project, and helped to shape the research questions.

Now that we have loaded all the data needed in this analysis the datasets need to be joined. First, we will join `litter_data` to `philly_tracts` and summarize the resulting dataset to get an average litter index value for each census tract. The resulting dataset `litter_data` will have \[\]. Then, to be able to plot the average litter index for each census tract on a map, `litter_avg` will be joined to `philly_tracts` by `GEOID10` to get the tract geometry back.

Then, the new dataset `litter_avg` will be joined to `census_vals` to get

\[explicitly mention grouping\]

This will allow for the litter index to be plotted on a map by census tract. Then, this will allow for liner regression to be done on the data to understand how litter correlates to household income, poverty level, median home value, median rent, and level of people who achieved a highschool diploma or equivalent.

```{R}
# code to join the litter shape data to tract data
litter_shp_trans <- st_transform(litter_shp, 4269)
philly_tracts_trans <- st_transform(philly_tracts, 4269)

shapes_joined <- st_join(litter_shp_trans, philly_tracts_trans, join = st_within)

# group and average litte data by census tract removing NAs
litter_avg <- shapes_joined |>
                    group_by(GEOID10) |> 
                    summarise(avg_litter = mean(STREET_CLA, na.rm = TRUE))

head(litter_avg)

# get census tract geometery back
litter_map <- st_drop_geometry(litter_avg) |> 
                left_join(philly_tracts, by = "GEOID10")
# class(litter_map)
litter_map <- st_as_sf(litter_map)

head(litter_map)

# find and filter out tracts with not enough data
no_data <- census_vals |>
  group_by(GEOID, estimate) |>
  filter (n() > 1) |>
  ungroup()

tract_list <- list(unique(no_data$GEOID10))

census_vals <- census_vals |> 
  filter(!tract_list %in% census_vals)

# pivot census data
census_vals <- census_vals |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = GEOID,
    names_from = measure,
    values_from = estimate
  )

# join to get a dataset that contains avg litter and all census values
litter_census <- left_join(litter_avg, census_vals, by = c("GEOID10" = "GEOID"))
litter_census <- st_drop_geometry(litter_census)

head(litter_census)

```

\[talk about doing regression\]

```{R}
# code for regression
# with and without include confounders

lm_income <- lm(avg_litter ~ median_household_income, data = litter_census)
summary(lm_income)

lm_poverty <- lm(avg_litter ~ num_people_in_poverty, data = litter_census)
summary(lm_poverty)

lm_home_value <- lm(avg_litter ~ median_home_value, data = litter_census)
summary(lm_home_value)

lm_rent <- lm(avg_litter ~ median_gross_rent, data = litter_census)
summary(lm_rent)

```

```{R}
# regression plot function adapted from: https://sejohnston.com/2012/08/09/a-quick-and-easy-function-to-plot-lm-results-in-r/
ggplotRegression <- function (lm, title, x, y) {
  
  df <- lm$model
  x_name <- names(df[2])
  y_name <- names(df[1])

  ggplot(df, aes_string(x = x_name, y = y_name)) + 
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
    labs(title = paste(title),
         subtitle = paste("Adj R2 = ", signif(summary(lm)$adj.r.squared, 5),
                       "Intercept =", signif(lm$coef[[1]],5 ),
                       " Slope =", signif(lm$coef[[2]], 5),
                       " P-Value =", signif(summary(lm)$coef[2,4], 5)),
         x = paste(x),
         y = paste(y))
}

# create the regression plots
ggplotRegression(lm_home_value, "Correlation Between Median Home Value and Litter", "Median Home Value", "Litter Index Value")

ggplotRegression(lm_income, "Correlation Between Median Household Income and Litter", "Median Household Income", "Litter Index Value")

ggplotRegression(lm_poverty, "Correlation Bewteen Number of People In Poverty and Litter", "People In Poverty", "Litter Index Value")

ggplotRegression(lm_rent, "Correlation Between Median Household Rent and Litter", "Median Household Rent", "Litter Index Value")

# report p-values here
```
